name: CleanEval (2007 shared task), CleanPortalEval (ppke-nlpg, portal-domain extension), and 'Multilingual Evaluation of Main Content Extractors for Web Pages' (SIGIR 2025) -- treated together as the lineage of small reference-based extraction benchmarks WCXB explicitly positions itself against.
kind: Three linked research results: a shared-task benchmark (CleanEval), a derivative benchmark dataset (CleanPortalEval), and a reproducibility/extension study (multilingual paper, SIGIR '25, building on Bevendorff et al.'s SIGIR '23 'An Empirical Comparison of Web Content Extraction Algorithms').
maturity: CleanEval: closed shared task, 2007, frozen and unmaintained -- still cited as de-facto standard purely for lack of a long-running replacement until WCXB (2026). CleanPortalEval: small maintained-on-GitHub companion dataset, no formal publication found distinct from its repo. Multilingual study: research prototype/reproducibility paper, published July 2025, part of the same webis.de/ChatNoir lineage as the SIGIR'23 Bevendorff comparison.
license: CleanEval: gold-standard extracted texts + source pages released for research use (exact license terms not confirmed in available material; treated as academic-use benchmark, predates modern open-data licensing norms). CleanPortalEval: hosted on GitHub (ppke-nlpg/CleanPortalEval), format-compatible with CleanEval, license not independently confirmed. Multilingual study: ACM-published paper (SIGIR 2025); code/data availability not confirmed from fetchable sources -- ACM DL blocked WebFetch with 403.
keeps_and_discards: CleanEval's task defines the reference as 'main content' text with boilerplate (nav, ads, footer, copyright) removed -- same content/boilerplate dichotomy as WCXB, but scored per-page against a single hand-annotated gold text rather than a diverse-archetype taxonomy. CleanPortalEval keeps the same input/gold format but samples MULTIPLE pages per domain (70 pages, 4 domains) specifically to test algorithms like GoldMiner that need cross-page pattern learning within a site -- i.e. it keeps domain redundancy that CleanEval and WCXB both deliberately minimize.
structure_preserved: CleanEval's original scoring (per ResearchGate table reference) used edit-distance and granularity parameters over sequences, not pure bag-of-words -- meaning it partially penalizes reordering, unlike WCXB's explicit bag-of-words choice. The multilingual study's own metric could not be confirmed in full via available fetches (see uncertain), but the Bevendorff et al. 2023 lineage it extends uses ROUGE-LSum (a sequence/longest-common-subsequence metric, order-sensitive) alongside Levenshtein edit distance -- both order- and structure-sensitive in a way WCXB's word-bag F1 is not.
interactive_elements: None of the three handle interactive elements -- CleanEval predates modern rich-interactive HTML (2007 corpus), CleanPortalEval inherits its format, and the multilingual study evaluates the same class of static-HTML main-content extractors.
interactive_state_fidelity: Not applicable to any of the three -- none model control state.
layout_awareness: None of the three benchmarks encode rendered layout in ground truth; all score against HTML/text source, consistent with the extractors under test (Readability-class heuristics) which themselves are largely layout-agnostic or use only DOM-structural heuristics (tag density, link density) rather than actual rendering geometry.
javascript_required: No for all three -- CleanEval's 2007 corpus predates the JS-heavy web entirely; CleanPortalEval inherits the same static-snapshot assumption; the multilingual study evaluates the same class of extractors (per Bevendorff lineage: Readability, Resiliparse, BoilerNet, Web2Text, Trafilatura-class tools) against static HTML, not rendered DOM.
evaluation_method: CleanEval: shared-task scoring via edit-distance/granularity-parameterized text alignment against a single human-annotated gold extraction per page (797 pages total, train/test 58/676-ish split per search summary -- note the split figures found are inconsistent across sources and flagged uncertain below). CleanPortalEval: same scoring script/format as CleanEval, applied to a portal-focused 70-page/4-domain set. Multilingual study (SIGIR 2025): reproduces and extends the Bevendorff et al. SIGIR'23 reproducibility methodology (ROUGE-LSum + Levenshtein against reference extractions) across five languages (Greek, English, Polish, Russian, Chinese) rather than English-only. All three remain REFERENCE-based (oracle) evaluations -- none is oracle-free, unlike this project's own interest.
corpus_size_and_origins: CleanEval: 797 pages total from 2007, gathered via Google queries on common search terms across diverse domains, with 737 websites tagged in the original task materials (search-summary figures for the train/test split were inconsistent -- one source states 58 train/676 test, treated as approximate and flagged uncertain). This is the benchmark this project's own fields.yaml explicitly cites: '58 English pages from 2007' for the training portion. CleanPortalEval: 70 pages from only 4 domains, deliberately domain-CONCENTRATED (opposite of WCXB's domain-diverse design) to test cross-page-pattern extractors. Multilingual study: corpus spans 5 languages (Greek, English, Polish, Russian, Chinese) -- exact per-language page counts and total corpus size were not confirmed from fetchable sources (ACM DL and ResearchGate both blocked full-text fetch); understood to extend the Bevendorff et al. 8-dataset combined corpus (which itself aggregates CleanEval, CleanPortalEval, and others into 'over 3,000 pages' per search-summary figures) into non-English languages.
reported_precision_recall: Exact current numeric CleanEval/CleanPortalEval scores per extractor were not independently re-confirmed from primary sources in this pass (PDF text extraction failed for the Bevendorff SIGIR'23 paper and the multilingual SIGIR'25 paper; both returned corrupted/compressed-stream text via WebFetch). What is established: WCXB's own comparison frames these older benchmarks as producing article-skewed, saturating scores (best systems around F1=0.93 on CleanEval-class corpora, matching WCXB's own article-only F1=0.932) that do not reveal the 0.41-0.84 spread WCXB found on non-article types -- i.e. the qualitative finding (old benchmarks saturate, hiding archetype variance) is well-evidenced even though this pass could not re-extract every numeric table.
independent_oracle: None in any of the three -- single or small-team human-annotated gold text is the sole reference in each case; no independent check outside the annotation process itself is described for CleanEval (2007, pre-LLM-assist era, so purely manual annotation) or CleanPortalEval. The multilingual study reproduces prior annotations/methodology rather than introducing a new oracle.
evidence_independence: CleanEval: shared-task format (multiple independent submitting teams), so scores are cross-validated across participants rather than vendor-self-reported -- a genuine independence strength for its era. CleanPortalEval: single research-group-produced dataset (ppke-nlpg), evidence independence not separately established. Multilingual study: academic reproducibility paper (webis.de group, same authors as the SIGIR'23 comparison), independent of any commercial extractor vendor -- comparable in independence posture to WCXB.
page_archetype_coverage: CleanEval and CleanPortalEval: essentially none -- both are article/generic-page corpora without WCXB's explicit 7-type taxonomy; CleanPortalEval's only structural axis is domain-repetition, not page-type diversity. This lack of archetype coverage is precisely the gap WCXB's paper cites as motivation. Multilingual study: adds LANGUAGE as a coverage axis but does not appear (from available fetches) to cross language with page-type archetype -- it extends the SAME article-centric corpus lineage into new languages rather than adding structural diversity.
script_and_locale_behaviour: This is the multilingual study's entire contribution: evaluation across Greek, English, Polish, Russian, and Chinese -- covering Latin (English, Polish), Cyrillic (Russian), Greek script, and CJK (Chinese) scripts, i.e. a genuine script-diversity test that CleanEval (English-only, 2007) and CleanPortalEval (format-inherited, presumably also Latin-script) do not attempt. Search-summary evidence indicates 'some extractors suffer significant drops in precision and recall on non-English or structurally irregular pages,' i.e. extractors tuned/tested primarily on English (which most heuristic tools -- Trafilatura, Readability, jusText -- historically are) show measurable non-English degradation, though this pass could not confirm exact per-language numeric drops or whether Chinese (no whitespace word boundaries) shows a categorically different failure mode from Cyrillic/Greek (whitespace-delimited but non-Latin alphabets).
leaks_outward: Not applicable to any of the three -- offline static-corpus benchmarks, no live capture telemetry.
mechanism_detectability: Not applicable -- static HTML corpora processed offline.
countermeasures: Not applicable -- no adversarial/privacy dimension in any of the three benchmarks.
measured_fidelity_cost: Not applicable -- no privacy-hardening tradeoff measured by any of the three.
gate_state_at_capture: Not tracked in CleanEval (2007, predates the modern consent-banner/paywall web) or CleanPortalEval; not confirmed for the multilingual study's corpus but presumed inherited from the same static-page-collection tradition, which does not systematically record gate state.
determinism: CleanEval/CleanPortalEval scoring scripts are themselves deterministic (edit-distance/granularity computation over fixed text), but ground truth in both is fixed at annotation time with no re-annotation-agreement figure confirmed. Multilingual study reproduces prior scoring methodology, presumably equally deterministic given fixed reference texts, though this pass could not confirm its exact metric definition (see uncertain).
determinism_across_versions: Not addressed by any of the three -- none test extractor score drift across tool library versions; this is a general gap across the whole extraction-benchmark literature this research pass has surfaced (also true of WCXB).
reproducibility: CleanEval: high in the narrow sense that the frozen 2007 corpus and gold texts are still cited/used 19 years later (its 'de facto standard' status until WCXB is itself the reproducibility evidence), though whether its own inter-annotator process is documented well enough for independent re-annotation is unclear. CleanPortalEval: reproducible in principle (fixed GitHub-hosted corpus, CleanEval-compatible format). Multilingual study: reproduces the Bevendorff et al. SIGIR'23 methodology as its explicit design choice, i.e. reproducibility-as-contribution -- extending known methodology to new languages rather than inventing a new metric, which is itself evidence the underlying method IS reproducible across research groups.
failure_modes: Documented qualitative failure mode across all three, most sharply in the multilingual study: extractors trained/tuned on English/Latin-script, article-shaped pages degrade on (a) non-article page types (WCXB's finding, which frames CleanEval as blind to) and (b) non-English/non-Latin scripts (the multilingual study's finding). CleanPortalEval's own motivating failure mode is that algorithms needing cross-page pattern learning (GoldMiner-style) cannot be fairly evaluated on CleanEval's domain-diverse, one-page-per-domain design.
failure_visibility: All three make failure visible through per-dataset (not per-archetype or fully per-language, based on available evidence) score reporting rather than a single number across all benchmarks combined -- a partial precedent for WCXB's more granular per-archetype table, though none of the three achieves WCXB's full type x system matrix.
scale_limits: Not applicable in a runtime sense -- all are fixed small corpora (CleanEval ~797 pages, CleanPortalEval 70 pages); no scale-cost claims made.
delta_cost_model: Not applicable -- static one-shot corpora, no incremental-update concept.
reanchoring_stability: Not applicable -- fixed text spans against fixed HTML snapshots, no re-anchoring.
adversarial_exposure: Not evaluated by any of the three -- none has an adversarial/injection page category; all predate or are orthogonal to the prompt-injection concern this project tracks.
provenance_carrying: Not evaluated -- gold-standard text spans carry no per-token provenance metadata in any of the three.
roundtrip_safety: Not evaluated by any of the three.
token_budget_and_ordering: CleanEval/CleanPortalEval's edit-distance-based scoring (as opposed to WCXB's word-bag choice) is at least ORDER-sensitive, meaning these older benchmarks are structurally closer to being able to assess an SLM-relevant ordering property than WCXB is -- though none of the three was designed with an SLM context-window/truncation use case in mind, so none reports token-budget behavior directly.
representation_cost: Not reported by any of the three -- none measures tokens-per-page or compression ratio.
what_could_be_adopted: Two narrow mechanisms: (1) CleanPortalEval's domain-concentration design (many pages from few domains) is a useful COMPLEMENT to WCXB's domain-diverse design for testing this project's own dedup/re-anchoring logic specifically on same-site page-to-page structural repetition, which is exactly the regime O(delta) and content-addressing claims need stress-tested. (2) the multilingual study's script-diversity axis (Greek/Cyrillic/CJK alongside Latin) should inform this project's own test-corpus construction for `script_and_locale_behaviour` claims, since a structure-agnostic, tag-plus-interactivity approach should in principle be MORE script-invariant than the extractors these benchmarks were built to test (none of which are structure-agnostic) -- that is a testable, currently unverified claim this project could validate against a small multilingual holdout.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY for all three -- each relies on hand-annotated 'main content' judgments (a region classification by another name), so none can certify a structure-agnostic extractor as correct, only reveal divergence from a heuristic majority judgment. no_layout_in_the_fold: NOT APPLICABLE / NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY -- none encodes geometry, so none can test layout-blind concealment filtering either way. o_delta: NOT APPLICABLE -- no incremental-update concept in any of the three. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS AS REAL-CORPUS SOURCES -- all three are real captured pages (2007 web for CleanEval, real portal sites for CleanPortalEval, real multilingual pages for the SIGIR'25 study), so reuse as replay fixtures violates nothing. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NOT APPLICABLE -- all three predate or are orthogonal to shadow-DOM capture. OVERALL VERDICT: adoptable in the actuator/evaluation layer only, and even there with real caveats -- CleanEval is stale (2007, pre-HTML5, no non-Latin coverage) and should be treated as a historical baseline rather than a current fidelity target; CleanPortalEval's narrow domain-concentration niche is the one piece worth borrowing directly for this project's own re-anchoring tests; the multilingual study's script-diversity methodology is worth replicating on this project's own corpus but its specific numeric findings could not be independently re-confirmed from the sources available in this research pass.
governance_signal_handling: Not addressed by any of the three -- CleanEval (2007) predates ai.txt/Content Signals/AIPREF entirely; CleanPortalEval and the multilingual study do not discuss governance signals in available material.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Not addressed by any of the three in available material -- none discusses lawful basis for retaining scraped page content, consistent with their status as pre-GDPR-era (CleanEval) or narrowly-scoped academic NLP benchmarks not framed around personal-data retention.
uncertain: corpus_size_and_origins (CleanEval train/test split figures were inconsistent across search-summary sources -- '58/676' vs a stated '797 total, 737 tagged'; the exact authoritative split was not independently re-verified against the original 2007 shared-task report)

reported_precision_recall (could not re-extract exact numeric tables from the Bevendorff SIGIR'23 paper or the multilingual SIGIR'25 paper -- both PDFs returned corrupted/unreadable text via WebFetch, and ACM DL blocked direct HTML fetch with 403)

script_and_locale_behaviour (multilingual study's exact per-language numeric findings, and whether Chinese specifically showed a distinct failure mode from Cyrillic/Greek, could not be confirmed from available sources)
license (none of the three benchmarks' precise redistribution/reuse license terms were independently confirmed)
